Effects of different microbial pretreatments on the anaerobic digestion of 
giant grass under anaerobic and microaerobic conditions 
Ligong Wang , Caiyan Liu , Baocheng Wei , Chao Song , Fanfan Cai , Guangqing Liu , 
Chang Chen * 
College of Chemical Engineering, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing 100029, China   
H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• Effects of loaded O2 in microbial pre­
treatment on anaerobic digestion were 
studied. 
• Higher yield of volatile fatty acids after 
microaerobic 
pretreatment 
was 
detected. 
• Anaerobic pretreatment by straw com­
posting inoculant had the highest 
methane yield. 
• Microbial responses to O2 loading varied 
significantly with microbial consortium.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Microbial pretreatment 
Giant grass 
Oxygen 
Methane yield 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Microbial pretreatment to lignocellulosic biomass for anaerobic digestion (AD) has achieved increased attention; 
however, the low efficiency and unclear mechanism of oxygen parameter affecting this process performance limit 
its practical application. In this study, five readily available microbial consortia were developed to analyze the 
influences of various oxygen concentrations during pretreatment process upon methane conversion efficiency 
and microbiota within AD of giant grass. Results found that anaerobic pretreatment by liquid or straw com­
posting inoculant, along with microaerobic pretreatment by cow manure at 10 mL/g VS oxygen concentration, 
obtained 23.1%, 24.4%, and 16.0% higher methane yields (275.3, 279.8, and 265.3 mL/g VS) than corre­
sponding untreated group, respectively. Microbial community analyses showed that microbial responses to ox­
ygen varied significantly with microbial consortium, which consequently caused different AD performances. The 
findings will enrich theoretical knowledge of microbial pretreatment and provide a technological guidance for 
efficient utilization of giant grass and other lignocellulosic biomasses.   
1. Introduction 
With a significant focus on the revolution of clean energy, renewable 
energy has increasingly been considered as a main selling point for 
promoting this transition. Renewable methane obtained by anaerobic 
digestion (AD) can be a potential source of heat or electricity with 
negligible environmental issues, and exhibits promise in alleviating the 
current dependence on energy generated from fossil fuels. In addition,

AD byproducts, such as biogas slurry (BS), can also be served as fertilizer 
(Peng et al., 2019). For these advantages, AD has attracted increasing 
attention and stimulated the rapid growth of AD enterprises worldwide. 
Nevertheless, a heavy dependence on feedstocks with seasonal charac­
teristics, such as corn stalk, wheat stalk, and cotton stalk, has become a 
serious challenge to the stability of continuously operating AD reactors 
and even to the sustainable advancement of the AD industry (Zheng 
et al., 2015). This increasing awareness of the lack of AD feedstocks has 
inspired research on new renewable materials for a wide range of 
applications. 
Giant grass (Pennisetum giganteum z.x.lin), an available energy crop 
with high productivity of over 500 tons/ha, is a perennial, renewable, 
and highly surviving herb mainly used to remediate environmental 
disturbances and produce biomass energy (Kang et al., 2016). Similar to 
conventional AD feedstocks, abundant fermentable organic matter, 
including cellulose and hemicellulose, is contained in giant grass and 
may allow this grass to serve as an attractive energy crop candidate (Liu 
et al., 2020). Nevertheless, the natural recalcitrance and high crystal­
linity of lignocellulose make hydrolytic enzymes with limited access to 
fermentable organic matter (Barua et al., 2018; Collard & Blin, 2014). As 
a result, current AD processes are usually designed and operated based 
on the inclusion of a pretreatment step, which results in acceleration of 
hydrolysis or solubilization of lignocellulose components, followed by a 
reliable and continuous acidogenesis and methanogenesis period (Barua 
et al., 2018). Pretreatments usually involve three methods, i.e., physical, 
chemical, and biological technology, in which microbial pretreatment 
may represent a more attractive option because of the energy-saving and 
eco-friendly characteristics (Wagner et al., 2013). Despite these advan­
tages, microbial reagents used for pretreatment, such as Phanerochaete 
chrysosporium, generally need to be cultivated for a long time (approx­
imately 20 days) under an oxygen supply (Zabed et al., 2019), which 
conflicts with the strict anaerobic condition of the subsequent AD pro­
cess. As such, in addition to the AD digester, another reactor must be 
designed for microbial pretreatment, which increases the burden on the 
investment side and presents an important barrier for practical appli­
cation. Therefore, alternative microbial pretreatment methods with 
short pretreatment period and cost-effective characteristic are urgently 
needed. 
Whether oxygen should be supplied in the microbial pretreatment 
process is highly controversial. For example, Amin et al. injected 0, 6, 
12, and 24 mL/g VS oxygen in the microbial pretreatment process of rice 
stalk and concluded that an oxygen supply of 12 mL/g VS was an 
appropriate stimulator of methane generation (Amin et al., 2021b). 
However, insignificant effects or even decreases in methane production 
have also been observed when oxygen was supplied to the microbial 
pretreatment process (Díaz et al., 2011; Lim & Wang, 2013; Okuda et al., 
2007). Evidently, microbial pretreatment under anaerobic and micro­
aerobic conditions has varied effects on AD performance; however, 
available explanations are extremely limited thus far. Therefore, it is 
necessary to perform comprehensive and systematic research to clarify 
the mechanism of microbial pretreatment under anaerobic and 
microaerobic conditions. 
This study selected five kinds of microbial reagents from various 
environments, namely, liquid inoculant (LI), straw composting inocu­
lant (SI), cow manure (CM), sheep dung (SD), and BS, all of which are 
readily available and contain different microorganisms for lignocellu­
lose hydrolysis, to pretreat giant grass to analyze the influences of varied 
oxygen concentrations upon the methane conversion efficiency and 
microbiota. Moreover, both the pretreatment and AD were performed in 
one reactor, which can decrease the invested cost and increase the 
operating convenience. Overall, this study was performed to (1) develop 
pretreatment strategies with short pretreatment period and cost- 
effective characteristic by utilizing different microbial consortia to 
enhance methane production, (2) identify the effects of microbial pre­
treatment under anaerobic and microaerobic conditions upon volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs) variations, kinetic characteristics of methane gener­
ation, and lignocellulosic structure alterations, and (3) determine mi­
crobial responses to oxygen from the pretreatment process to the AD 
period to identify the mechanism involved in microbial pretreatment 
under anaerobic and microaerobic conditions. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Feedstocks and inoculum 
Giant grass was purchased on a local farm, situated in Hebei Province 
within China, and initially processed using a chopper to a length range 
of 1–2 cm and subsequently milled to cross a 0.5 cm sieve before usage. 
LI and SI are commercially applicable for stalk compost. CM and SD 
were kindly provided from a farm within Shunyi District of Beijing and 
using deionized water so that these materials could be evenly distrib­
uted. BS and inoculum have been fully described previously (Ning et al., 
2018). Table 1 presents the physical–chemical characteristics of the 
abovementioned materials. 
2.2. Microbial pretreatment and anaerobic digestion 
Glass bottles were developed into pretreatment reactors (total vol­
ume = 500 mL, effective volume = 100 mL). First, 2 g/L SI, CM, SD, and 
BS and 10 mL of LI were applied as microbial consortia to pretreat 10 g/L 
giant grass on a volatile solids (VS) basis, and then deionized water was 
added to the reactor until an effective volume of 100 mL was reached. 
The air inside the pretreatment reactor was initially removed with the 
help of a nitrogen purge for each pretreatment reactor, followed by a 
quick sealing operation using rubber stoppers. Later, oxygen was sepa­
rately injected at concentrations of 0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mL/g VS (on a VS 
basis) to create anaerobic and microaerobic conditions for the respective 
pretreatment groups and then preserved for 5 days at 37 ◦C. During this 
period, manual mixing of the reactor once every day was required for 
even blending, and the oxygen concentration in the headspace was 
monitored.

to each reactor for AD at 10 g VS/L to ensure a favorable biodegradation 
rate (Amin et al., 2021b). The effective volume was adjusted to 200 mL 
with deionized water. To exclude the background methane yield from 
the pretreatment reagent for an accurate experimental value, control 
groups that included respective microbial consortia and inoculum were 
set for comparison. Meanwhile, untreated groups that included raw 
giant grass, inoculum, and respective microbial consortia were also set. 
After an adjustment of the initial pH to 7.5 with a NaOH solution, all AD 
reactors were flushed with nitrogen for 3–5 min to remove air for an 
anaerobic condition, and then subjected to 47 days of cultivation at a 
temperature of 37 ◦C. The reactor was shaken manually twice per day to 
ensure full contact of individual components. The daily biogas accu­
mulation was computed based on a previously described method (Ning 
et al., 2018). 
2.3. Analysis methodology 
The measurement to quantify the values of total solids (TS) and VS 
followed previously reported procedures (Ning et al., 2018), while 
microelement (C and H) qualification was fulfilled with Germany’s 
Vario EL CUBE element analyzer. The lignocellulosic components were 
characterized by means of the Van Soest procedure (Van Soest et al., 
1991). The whole procedure for determining VFAs concentrations and 
compositions was accomplished by means of an Agilent 7890A gas 
chromatograph manufactured in USA. Quantification of oxygen during 
the pretreatment process and methane in the biogas was performed with 
an Agilent 7890B gas chromatograph (USA), and a relevant analytical 
column (Agilent Hayesep Q). Helium at 34.5 kPa pressure was used as 
the carrier gas during the operation. The biodiversity and structural 
analyses of microbial communities are detailed in the Supplementary 
Material. Origin software, single-factor analysis of variance, and circos 
online service have been used for the data analyses. 
2.4. Kinetic and microstructure analysis 
To further comprehensively assess the AD performance of giant 
grass, both a modified Gompertz model and a first-order dynamic model 
were applied to the accumulated methane production data obtained 
over 47 days, as described previously (Ning et al., 2018). 
The lignocellulosic components and structural changes in giant grass 
with or without pretreatment were primarily determined based on the 
Van Soest method, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and Fourier transform 
infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The XRD system (Bruker, Germany) is 
equipped with a Cu Kα target at a scanning rate of 5.0◦/min, with var­
iations between 5◦and 90◦, and the FTIR system (Thermo Fisher Nicolet 
6700, USA) is equipped with a DLATGS detector operating at scanning 
wavelengths in the range of 400 cm−1 to 4000 cm−1. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effects of variant oxygen concentrations in the pretreatment process 
upon the yields of volatile fatty acids 
VFAs, mainly acetic acid, propionic acid, butyric acid, valeric acid, 
etc., are well known as the primary products of the acidogenesis phase 
and the key carbon sources for yielding methane (Chen et al., 2012). 
Here, the concentrations and main components of VFAs after different 
microbial pretreatments at various oxygen concentrations were detec­
ted, as displayed in Fig. 1. The VFAs concentrations were found at 
various levels among all pretreatment groups, with a higher VFAs level 
observed for the SI, CM, SD, and BS pretreatments than the LI pre­
treatment. This result may be related to the effect of innate differences in 
the composition and microbial species within the pretreatment agents. 
Moreover, when oxygen was supplied to the pretreatment process, the 
likelihood of hydrolysis products transforming into VFAs was generally 
enhanced, which was similar with prior observations (Eryildiz and 
LukitawesaTaherzadeh, 2020; Khan et al., 2016). 
The VFAs concentrations from LI pretreatment reached a peak 
(1263.3 mg/L) at an oxygen concentration of 10 mL/g VS, and primarily 
corresponded to acetic acid, which was quite different from the results of 
other pretreatment groups. The VFAs concentrations of the SI pretreat­
ment increased from 2001.4 to 4465.9 mg/L when the oxygen concen­
tration ranged from 0 to 10 mL/g VS and subsequently decreased but 
remained higher (2017.4–3374.7 mg/L) than that under anaerobic 
condition. Among the compositions, acetic acid was expected to take the 
dominant position in a range from 1482 to 3533.8 mg/L. When the 
oxygen concentration was enhanced to 10 mL/g VS, the yields of acetic 
acid and butyric acid received maximum values of 3533.8 and 622.0 
mg/L, respectively. At oxygen concentrations of 10 and 20 mL/g VS, 
additional ethanol products were detected at concentrations of 45.2 and 
15.1 mg/L, respectively. The VFAs concentrations during CM pretreat­
ment at oxygen concentrations of 0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 mL/g VS were 
1932.8, 3636.5, 5590.3, 2471.1, and 1718.0 mg/L, respectively. The 
production of VFAs started to increase after oxygen addition during the 
pretreatment process and achieved the highest value at 10 mL/g VS of 
oxygen concentration, corresponding to 2.89-fold than that of the 
anaerobic pretreatment. This result might be associated with the better 
microbial growth of the CM reagent under microaerobic conditions 
(Jackson et al., 1970). While, the suitable oxygen concentration for the 
SD reagent was 5 mL/g VS, resulting in a VFAs production of 3606.7 mg/ 
L, in which acetic acid accounted for 2699.5 mg/L. In comparison with 
other pretreatments, BS at any oxygen concentration produced higher 
VFAs production, which changed from 4734.6 to 8388.4 mg/L. The high 
output of VFAs might be a consequence of the abundant bacteria related 
to the hydrolysis and acidogenesis in BS. 
3.2. Cumulative methane yield analysis 
Effects of oxygen introduced at different loadings during the mi­
crobial pretreatment process on cumulative methane yield (CMY) are 
indicated in Fig. 2. The experimental methane yield (EMY), an indica­
tion of the maximum CMY, has been applied as an indicator for AD 
performance evaluation. The anaerobic pretreatment by LI resulted in a 
higher rate of methane accumulation, which reached an EMY of 275.3 
mL/g VS (Fig. 2A). Oxygen supplied at 5 mL/g VS to the LI pretreatment 
process led to a decrease in the EMY to 230.6 mL/g VS, and an increase 
in oxygen from 10 to 40 mL/g VS led the EMY to vary from 249.4 to 
272.6 mL/g VS. Anaerobic pretreatment by LI produced the highest EMY 
increase (23.1%) in relation to the untreated group (223.6 mL/g VS). In 
the SI pretreatment groups (Fig. 2B), and it reached 279.8 mL/g VS 
without oxygen in the SI pretreatment process with an increase of 24.4%

either 5 mL/g VS oxygen or 10 mL/g VS oxygen. Thereafter, the EMY 
peaked at 281.3 mL/g VS under continuous increases in the oxygen 
concentration to 20 mL/g VS, with the highest increase of 25.0% relative 
to the untreated group, and then the value decreased to 260.8 mL/g VS 
at 40 mL/g VS oxygen. Notably, the differences in EMY between SI 
pretreatments under anaerobic conditions and 20 mL/g VS oxygen 
concentration were limited. In other words, oxygen was not recom­
mended for the SI pretreatment process because of the extremely limited 
enhancement in EMY. The EMYs of the CM pretreatment at 0, 5, 10, 20, 
and 40 mL/g VS oxygen concentrations were 259.5, 246.6, 265.3, 230.5, 
and 249.0 mL/g VS, respectively, which represented increases of 
0.8–16.0% relative to the untreated group (228.6 mL/g VS). Methane 
production showed the highest increase at an oxygen concentration of 
10 mL/g VS, probably as a result of the highest VFAs concentration 
achieved during pretreatment process under this condition. Regarding 
the SD pretreatment group, the maximum EMY of 266.3 mL/g VS 
occurred under anaerobic conditions, which was a 9.9% increase 
compared with that of the untreated group (242.2 mL/g VS). Moreover, 
giant grass pretreated with SD at 40 mL/g VS oxygen unexpectedly 
showed an inferior methane output of 233.1 mL/g VS compared with 
untreated grass. Consistent with the SD pretreatment groups, the 
application of a microaerobic strategy for the BS pretreatment process 
also caused a reduction in EMY. In the BS pretreatment group, anaerobic 
condition achieved the highest EMY of 260.2 mL/g VS, which repre­
sented an improvement of 14.8% in relation to untreated group (226.7 
mL/g VS). This were likely associated with the relatively higher VFAs 
concentrations (more than 5000 mg/L) during the anaerobic pretreat­
ment process. 
In short, higher EMYs were commonly determined for the LI, SI, and 
CM pretreatment groups at optimum conditions, which represented in­
creases of 23.1, 24.4, and 16.0% than the untreated groups, respectively. 
Fu et al. analyzed the performance of microaerobic pretreatment under 
thermophilic condition and attained a maximum increase of 16.2% at an 
oxygen concentration of 5 mL/g VS with respect to untreated straw (Fu 
et al., 2015). Similarly, Xu et al. performed a biological pretreatment 
using a pure bacterial system with or without introducing oxygen for AD 
of corn straw, and received the maximum EMY of 270.8 mL/g VS at an

operating oxygen concentration of 5 mL/g VS, along with a 17.4% in­
crease relative to the untreated system (Xu et al., 2018). Comparatively, 
the enhanced methane production observed in these previous studies 
could be achieved using CM at suitable oxygen concentration in the 
present work, not to mention LI and SI pretreatment. Furthermore, using 
CM could reduce pollution by transforming waste material into a useful 
end product while also reducing the pretreatment cost. Therefore, future 
AD applications should focus on these readily available pretreatment 
agents. One more thing, after an AD run of 25 days, the CMY from all 
groups amounted to 80.2–86.2% of the final EMY. This implied that if 
the digestion time were designed as 25 days instead of 47 days, the size 
of future AD reactor could be decreased by 46.8% by sacrificing only 
13.8–19.8% of methane production. 
3.3. Kinetic and microstructure analysis 
The understanding of kinetic characteristics is important for future 
modifications of technical procedures (Xu et al., 2015). Thus, the clas­
sical modified Gompertz and first-order dynamic models are imple­
mented. As pointed out in the resulting Table 2, the reliability of further 
analysis using the simulated kinetic parameters was confirmed because 
the correlation coefficients (R2) of these two models were greater than 
0.98. Consistent with the EMY data, the simulated maximum CMY (B0) 
from both models varied significantly with changes in either the pre­
treatment agent or oxygen loading. Commonly used to indicate the lag 
phase, λ tended to decrease after the SD, SI, and BS pretreatments and 
increased to different extents after the CM and LI pretreatments, as 
shown in the illustration in Fig. 2. The hydrolysis rate (k) was expected 
to increase in the pretreatment groups compared with the untreated 
samples, and the highest hydrolysis rate generally corresponded to the 
highest EMY for each pretreatment group. 
To better understand the characteristic changes in giant grass before 
and after oxygen loading in the pretreatment process, XRD and FTIR 
techniques were used to provide valuable information, such as the 
crystalline degree of cellulose and the chemical composition. The LI, SI, 
and CM groups had high EMY values and were selected for the XRD and 
FTIR analyses. The patterns included two peaks (see Supplementary 
Material) at 2θ = 16◦and 2θ = 22◦for cellulose I crystals and 2θ = 18◦
for amorphous substances. Most peaks at 2θ = 22◦for the pretreated 
samples decreased to different extents, thus indicating that the crystal­
line degree of cellulose was transforming to some extent. Amorphous 
cellulose is more easily utilized, and the intensity approximately at 2θ =
18◦was detected for the pretreated samples; however, it was not 
observed in the untreated samples. This result was indicating that pre­
treatment certainly reduce the crystalline degree of cellulose, as shown 
in the Supplementary Material. The peaks observed in the FTIR spectra 
could be explained as follows (see Supplementary Material): 1730 cm−1 
for the C = O vibration, 1515 cm−1 for the benzene framework, and 900 
cm−1 for the O–H stretching vibration (Correia et al., 2013; Ding et al., 
2012; Faulon et al., 1994; Pandey & Pitman, 2004). Peaks at 1730 cm−1 
correlated well with the hemicellulose composition (Ding et al., 2012; 
Pandey & Pitman, 2004), and obvious alterations in this peak were not 
found between anaerobic- and microaerobic-pretreated giant grass, 
although the peak decreased compared to that of the untreated giant 
grass. Hemicellulose has been widely studied as a readily decomposing 
component; thus, its dissolution after pretreatment could be helpful for 
VFAs and EMY production, as previously observed. On the other hand, 
peaks at 1515 cm−1 were the characteristic of lignin (Pandey & Pitman, 
2004). A decrease in the height of this peak was observed for all pre­
treated giant grass relative to the untreated sample. Lignin could greatly 
hinder cellulose degradation; thus, its removal has attracted extensive 
attention. Therefore, all pretreatments were expected to facilitate

CM and SI pretreatments under anaerobic and microaerobic conditions 
did not show a significant difference in the peak at 1515 cm−1. However,

conditions compared with anaerobic conditions for the LI pretreatment. 
Consequently, anaerobic LI pretreatment could favor methane produc­

which was consistent with the information in Supplementary Material. 
3.4. Biodiversity and microbial communities analyses 
3.4.1. Biodiversity and species abundance distribution 
LI pretreatment groups at 0 and 10 mL/g VS, SI pretreatment groups 
at 0 and 20 mL/g VS, and CM pretreatment groups at 0 and 10 mL/g VS 
were selected for microbial communities’ analyses due to the relatively 
good EMY performance. Various indicators, including the OTU number, 
Shannon index, Simpson index, ACE, and Chao 1 estimator, can repre­
sent the level of microbial diversity and richness, and were compared 
(see Supplementary Material). A coverage value over 0.98 indicated 
reliability for further analyses. It was suggested that bacteria did 
generally occur in higher Shannon index, ACE, and Chao 1 estimator 
than archaea, and therefore in predominant microbial community from 
pretreatment until AD process. The CM group had higher species di­
versity and richness during the pretreatment process and higher Shan­
non index and ACE estimator values for bacteria, which were likely the 
inherently abundant microorganisms in CM. Additionally, the high 
values observed for CM might explain the higher VFA concentrations 
shown in Fig. 1. Except for the ACE estimator value obtained in the LI 
and CM pretreatment processes, the Shannon index and ACE estimator 
of bacteria from the remaining experimental groups showed enhance­
ments with the introduction of oxygen in the pretreatment process. After 
AD, the Shannon index and ACE estimator of bacteria showed different 
degrees of increase among the different pretreatment processes, which 
was likely caused by the appearance of new bacterial species associated 
with AD. Archaea play a critical role in the final methane conversion 
efficiency. Compared to anaerobic conditions, the ACE and Chao 1 
estimator values of the digestate from microaerobic CM-pretreated giant 
grass increased, while those from microaerobic LI-pretreated giant grass 
did not show significant differences, which may explain the higher EMY 
resulted from microaerobic pretreatment by CM and anaerobic pre­
treatment by LI. 
3.4.2. Bacterial analysis on the general level 
Bacterial relative abundance (RA) on the general level in the pre­
treatment agent, during the pretreatment process, and after AD was 
detected, as shown in Fig. 3. The dominant bacterium in the LI reagent 
was Bacillus (88.5% RA), which then decreased to 54.0% and 46.4% 
during the pretreatment under anaerobic and microaerobic condition, 
respectively. The RA of Bacillus finally decreased to 0.2% and 0.5% after 
the AD period, respectively. Generally, anaerobic conditions could 
enrich members of this genus more than microaerobic conditions in the 
pretreatment process. Bacillus is an aerobic or facultative anaerobe that 
can release many extracellular enzymes, such as cellulase, xylanase, 
amylase, and peroxidase (Carrillo-Reyes et al., 2016; Zabed et al., 2019). 
Cellulases are important enzymes that biocatalyze depolymerization of 
cellulosic biomass into fermentable sugars, while xylanase can convert 
hemicellulose into oligosaccharides and release easily degradable nu­
trients from lignocellulose biomass (Carrillo-Reyes et al., 2016; Zabed 
et al., 2019). Peroxidase is highly linked to lignin decomposition (Car­
rillo-Reyes et al., 2016). Thus, Bacillus had a strong relationship with

cellulose and lignin decomposition, and an increase in RA under 
anaerobic conditions led to greater lignocellulose degradation compared 
with that under microaerobic conditions. This result could be reflected 
in the analyses of lignocellulose alteration (see Supplementary Mate­
rial), where the hemicellulose content was generally released after the 
anaerobic pretreatment by LI and could be readily used in the subse­
quent AD period. Additionally, the RA of the second most dominant 
genus (Enterobacter) was significantly different under anaerobic condi­
tions (19.7%) and microaerobic conditions (12.5%). After the AD 
period, this genus was scarcely detected. Enterobacter, as a facultative 
anaerobe, was reported to belong to the family of Enterobacteriaceae, and 
previous literature commonly applied anaerobic condition to promote 
the enrichment of this bacterium, which might certainly explain why 
Enterobacter has a higher RA under anaerobic condition than that under 
microaerobic condition (Maru et al., 2016). The function of Enterobacter 
includes transforming multiple carbon sources into acetic acid and H2 
(Maru et al., 2016), and has a potential beneficial effect in cooperation 
with methanogenic bacteria. These results indicated that applying 
anaerobic conditions could help to enrich Enterobacter during LI pre­
treatment process and thus might benefit subsequent AD performance. 
The third most dominant genus is Lactobacillus, which is strongly posi­
tively correlated with the conversion of a wide range of sugars into 
lactate (Hatti-Kaul et al., 2018). This genus was more prevalent under 
microaerobic conditions (20.9%) than under anaerobic conditions 
(4.8%). Moreover, the bacteria Clostridium sensu stricto 1, Sed­
imentibacter, Ruminococcaceae incertae sedis, Petrimonas, VadinBC27, 
Pelotomaculum, Azoarcus, Syntrophomonas, and Thermovirga did not 
show significant growth in the pretreatment procedure but began to 
increase in the AD process. These microbes have the potential to trans­
form several sugars and organic acids as acetic acid, butyrate, and H2 to 
enhance the subsequent methanogenesis rate (Costabile et al., 2017; 
Grabowski et al., 2005; Li et al., 2018; Morrison et al., 2016; Nordhoff 
et al., 2005; Xie et al., 2014). Notably, the RA of these genera was 
generally higher in the digestate from anaerobic pretreatment than that 
microaerobic pretreatment by LI, which possibly played an important 
role in the greater accumulation of methane for the LI pretreatment 
group under anaerobic condition (Fig. 2). 
The dominant genus in the SI agent was Staphylococcus at a RA of 
51.4%. During the microbial pretreatment process, this bacterium dis­
appeared; Enterobacter, Kosakonia, and Lactococcus started to develop as 
the dominant genera, and showed greater RA values under anaerobic 
pretreatment conditions (36.0, 16.9, and 11.5%, respectively) than 
under the microaerobic pretreatment conditions (18.5, 10.3, and 1.6%, 
respectively). However, Enterobacter, Kosakonia, and Lactococcus were 
almost undetected after AD process. As previously mentioned, Entero­
bacter could benefit subsequent AD performance; therefore, the finding 
of a higher methane yield from the giant grass pretreated by anaerobic SI 
pretreatment was reasonable (Fig. 2). Kosakonia is a facultative 
anaerobe, and is effective in the fixation of nitrogen nutrients and the 
production of xylanase (Chin et al., 2017). Nitrogen fixation might 
benefit the growth of hydrolytic microorganisms, while the generation 
of xylanase will promote the conversion of fiber into oligosaccharides 
and the release of fermentable nutrients from lignocellulose biomass 
(Chin et al., 2017). For Lactococcus, it is a part of the group of lactic acid 
bacteria, and is likely to induce a significant promotion on the genera­
tion of lactic acid, which was a useful source of VFAs (Casalta & Montel, 
2008). Therefore, the higher RA of Enterobacter, Kosakonia, and Lacto­
coccus probably laid a foundation for the observed higher methane 
production of anaerobically pretreated giant grass by SI. After the AD 
process, the dominant genera of the SI pretreatment groups included 
VadinBC27, Ruminococcaceae incertae sedis, Fastidiosipila, and Clostridium 
sensu stricto 1. Comparably, the VadinBC27, Ruminococcaceae incertae 
sedis, and Fastidiosipila presented higher RA after the AD period of giant 
grass under anaerobic condition (18.8, 9.6, and 10.9%, respectively) 
compared with the microaerobic condition (12.7, 8.2, and 9.5%, 
respectively). The VadinBC27 belonged to the Rikenellaceae family of the 
Bacteroidetes phylum and was identified as a major factor for methane 
production (Rautio et al., 2003). It was recognized as degrading amino 
acids in syntrophic association with hydrogenotrophic methanogens, 
and the 48.0% increase in the RA for anaerobic condition than micro­
aerobic condition might also played an important role in enhancing 
methane production. Ruminococcaceae incertae sedis hydrolyzes and di­
gests carbohydrates, such as cellulose and hemicellulose, to form short- 
chain fatty acids (Costabile et al., 2017), while Fastidiosipila is important 
for generating precursor for methane synthesis (Falsen et al., 2005). 
Clostridium sensu stricto 1 is one of the most common genera in AD and 
generally acts on several types of sugars for preparing methanogenesis 
precursors, and it therefore has the added benefit of reducing the 
starting time for AD (Lanjekar et al., 2015). However, the significant 
genera including Clostridium sensu stricto 1, Ruminococcaceae incertae 
sedis, and Fastidiosipila, did not have significant differences between the 
microaerobic and anaerobic SI pretreatment process. Over the whole, 
the microaerobic pretreatment decreased the RA of Enterobacter and 
Kosakonia and negatively influenced the enrichment with respect to the 
vadinBC27 in AD process. Therefore, oxygen loading was not recom­
mended during the SI pretreatment process. 
Bacterial genera such as Acinetobacter, Proteiniphilum, Petrimonas, 
Fastidiosipila, and VadinBC27 are common in CM. Acinetobacter, Protei­
niphilum, and Petrimonas are most likely available for the decomposition 
of lignin, protein, and hemicellulose, respectively (Iino et al., 2009; Iyer 
& Mahadevan, 2002; Wongfaed et al., 2020). Most bacteria from Aci­
netobacter were aerobic, therefore during CM2, the RA of Acinetobacter 
generally increased, with values increasing from 4.5 to 14.2% compared 
to that with the CM reagent. This finding indicated that oxygen in the 
CM pretreatment might play an important role in lignin degradation; 
therefore, VFAs concentrations would increase under microaerobic 
condition (Fig. 1). However, this genus was rarely detected after the AD 
period, which might be related to its aerobic characteristics. Changes in 
the RA of Proteiniphilum and Petrimonas differed relative to that of Aci­
netobacter, and tended to decreased to a negligible level across both the 
CM pretreatment process and AD period. Fastidiosipila has been shown to 
promote the accumulation of acetic and butyric acids, known as pre­
cursors for methane production. Fastidiosipila and VadinBC27 tended to 
change similarly; initially, the RA was hardly detected in pretreatment 
process regardless of anaerobic or microaerobic condition, followed by 
an increase after AD period and the abundance under anaerobic and 
microaerobic condition did not vary significantly. Clostridium sensu 
stricto 1 is important for converting multiple sugars into methanogenic 
precursors (Morrison et al., 2016; Xie et al., 2014). These bacteria were 
not observed in the CM, and the increase in the RA was not obvious in 
the pretreatment stage; although a significant increase occurred after 
the AD period, the RA under anaerobic and microaerobic condition was 
not significantly different. In general, a limited oxygen supply (10 mL/g 
VS) would achieve a high RA of the Acinetobacter during CM pretreat­
ment process, and might alleviate the lignin resistance to lignocellulosic 
hydrolysis. Therefore, VFAs were efficiently produced during the 
microaerobic CM pretreatment process while considerably high EMY 
values were observed in the AD of giant grass under this condition. 
3.4.3. Archaeal analysis on the general level 
The distribution and RA values of archaea between the anaerobic 
and microaerobic conditions for the LI, SI, and CM groups are shown in 
Fig. 4. The prominent genera in this study were mainly Methanospirillum 
(52.7%), Methanobacterium (32.7%), Methanosaeta (12.0%), and Meth­
anosarcina (1.75%) in the LI reagent; Candidatus nitrososphaera (31.7%), 
Methanosarcina (25.6%), Methanoculleus (20.6%), Methanomassiliicoccus 
(5.9%), Methanobacterium (5.5%), and Methanosaeta (4.8%) in the SI 
reagent; and Methanobrevibacterium (68.8%), Methanosaeta (18.7%), 
Methanoculleus (5.0%), Methanosarcina (3.7%), and Candidatus meth­
anomethylophilus (1.7%) in the CM reagent. Methanosaeta functions via 
the acetoclastic pathway to produce methane (Amin et al., 2021a), while

been found to function by hydrogenotrophic pathways and uses multiple 
materials, including H2, CO2, and formate, to form methane, and 
Methanomassiliicoccus is widely known to function via the methylo­

anosaeta, Methanoculleus, and Methanomassiliicoccus detected under 
anaerobic condition was 73.5, 19.8, 3.1, and 2.8%, while under micro­
aerobic condition, it changed to 77.6, 20.5, 0.9, and 0.6%, respectively. 
Obviously, the response of microbial structures to oxygen varied with 
the microbial reagent, and thus, the microbial reagent might be a po­
tential parameter influencing microorganisms within the digestion 
period. 
4. Conclusions 
This study identified commonly higher VFAs yield after microaerobic 
pretreatment, and 23.1%, 24.4%, and 16% increase in methane pro­
duction than untreated respectively after anaerobic pretreatment by LI, 
anaerobic pretreatment by SI, and microaerobic pretreatment by CM at 
10 mL/g VS oxygen concentration. Also, microbial response to oxygen 
depended on the microbial consortia. For example, anaerobic condition 
benefited the enrichment of Bacillus and Enterobacter during LI pre­
treatment process, which might promote the conversion of lignocellu­
lose and enhanced AD performance. While, optimal oxygen could enrich 
lignin-degrading bacteria (Acinetobacter) in CM pretreatment process, 
thereby observing high EMY value under this condition.
